1. Core Clinical Tension: A 43-year-old HIV-negative male presents with a 1-year history of recurrent cough, pericardial and pleural effusions, polyarthralgia, extreme leukocytosis (WBC 41.23 × 10^9/L), HLA-B27 positivity, multiple suppurative skin/soft tissue masses, osteolytic rib and vertebral bone destruction, and pelvic abscesses. He had previously been misdiagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and ankylosing spondylitis. The critical tension is distinguishing an aggressive endemic dimorphic fungal infection in an immunocompetent patient from disseminated tuberculosis, pyogenic osteomyelitis, or autoimmune spondyloarthropathy.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs upon completion of admission triage, physical examination, baseline laboratory panels, and multi-site CT/MRI imaging at the referral center, prior to hospital transfer treatment trials, bone marrow aspiration smear, galactomannan testing, lymph node biopsy, and pus mNGS.
3. Differential Distinctions: Disseminated tuberculosis was the primary misdiagnosis but was ruled out by negative IGRA, negative BALF Xpert/TB-DNA, lack of response to antitubercular therapy, and negative lymph node histology. Ankylosing spondylitis was ruled out because HLA-B27 cannot account for destructive osteolysis, polyserositis, and purulent subcutaneous abscesses. Pyogenic bacterial sepsis was excluded by failure of meropenem and sterile routine bacterial cultures.
case_prompt:
A 43-year-old male presents with recurrent cough and sputum production for 1 year, accompanied by joint pain involving all extremities for 10 months. One year prior, he was hospitalized elsewhere for cough, sputum, and fever, where thick brown pericardial and pleural fluid was aspirated; empirical therapy for chronic granulomatous infection was administered without symptom relief. Three months prior to admission, he developed a cranial mass that resolved after antimicrobial therapy. One month prior to admission, multiple masses developed on his head, neck, axillae, arms, and abdomen; an arm lesion spontaneously ruptured, draining yellow-white pus. Epidemiological history is notable for long-term residence and work as a driver in Myanmar 4 years ago, along with consumption of bamboo rats.

On physical examination, the patient has two masses measuring 4 × 5 cm on the neck, a 4 × 3 cm mass in the left axilla, and three firm 1 × 1 cm masses on the right upper arm. Auscultation reveals bilateral moist pulmonary rales.

Laboratory investigations reveal a white blood cell count of 41.23 × 10^9/L with 88.4% neutrophils, hemoglobin 89 g/L, C-reactive protein 129.4 mg/L, and procalcitonin 6.92 ng/mL. Hepatic and nutritional panels show total bilirubin 43.3 µmol/L (direct 30.5 µmol/L), albumin 13.9 g/L, and globulin 54.1 g/L. Immunological testing demonstrates CD4+ T cell count 1730 cells/µL, CD8+ T cell count 1325 cells/µL, negative HIV antibody, negative interferon-gamma release assay, negative parasite antibodies, negative autoimmune antibodies, positive direct anti-human globulin test, and positive HLA-B27.

Chest CT demonstrates scattered spots, nodules, and strip shadows with uneven density and blurred edges in both lungs, multiple enlarged mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes, and bone destruction of the left 4th rib with adjacent soft-tissue swelling (largest measuring 7.6 × 4.7 cm in the axilla). Hip CT shows bilateral joint fluid accumulation and bone erosion. Bronchoscopy shows non-specific chronic inflammatory changes. Spine and pelvic MRI reveals patchy altered T1/T2 signals with marked enhancement in the thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and iliac bones, with abscess formation around the right sacroiliac and bilateral hip joints.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Chronic cough, polyserositis, multifocal osteolysis, lymphadenopathy, and cold abscesses led to an initial clinical misdiagnosis of tuberculosis; however, interferon-gamma testing was negative, empirical antitubercular therapy failed, BALF Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA/Xpert assays were negative, and lymph node biopsy showed no granulomas or acid-fast bacilli.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: During hospitalization, the interferon-gamma test of this patient was negative, and the Mantoux test had not been performed... the initial hospital considered a clinical diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis and administered anti-tuberculosis treatment. However, the patient's symptoms were not well relieved.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Extremity polyarthralgia, sacroiliac and spinal abnormalities, and a positive HLA-B27 test prompted a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis; however, marked bone destruction, extensive soft-tissue abscesses, negative autoimmune antibodies, and purulent draining sinuses indicated an aggressive infectious process rather than an autoimmune inflammatory spondylopathy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The lesions showed slightly high signal intensity on T2 fat suppression and were significantly enhanced by enhanced scan, suggesting that the possibility of infectious lesions was high. An abscess formed around the right sacroiliac joint and bilateral hip joints

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Marked leukocytosis (41.23 × 10^9/L) with neutrophil predominance and purulent draining abscesses suggested acute pyogenic bacterial infection; however, broad-spectrum meropenem therapy was ineffective, and aspirate cultures were sterile for bacteria.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: intravenous meropenem was administered. However, after 4 days, there was no improvement... Culture of the subcutaneous abscess puncture showed no bacterial growth and no Candida growth.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot was informed by the patient's exposure history (extended residence in Myanmar and bamboo rat consumption), positive Aspergillus galactomannan cross-reactivity, bone marrow aspirate demonstrating fungal hyphae, and definitive identification of Talaromyces marneffei via metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of pus aspirated from the subcutaneous mass.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: In addition, he had a history of bamboo rat consumption... the Aspergillus galactomannan test was positive. Therefore, we considered the possibility of fungal infection... Additionally, a previous culture of the bone marrow fluid showed the presence of fungal hyphae... Subsequently, pus from the skin mass was aspirated for mNGS, which confirmed the T. marneffei infection.

editor_comments: Presentation halts strictly prior to transfer interventions, bone marrow smear, galactomannan testing, and mNGS. Zero spoilers or pathogen names in case_prompt. Differential evaluations are fully grounded in the article with exact verbatim quotes.
